children.text: athāto dvividhauṣadhavijñānīyamadhyāyaṃ vyākhyāsyāma iti ha smāhurātreyādayo maharṣayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Now then, we shall explain the chapter on the knowledge of the two kinds of medicine. Thus, indeed, said the great seers beginning with <s>Ātreya</s>.
Medicine is of two kinds: that which promotes strength and that which destroys disease.
And both of these also have the nature of both.
But the designation is made according to predominance.
There, the strength-promoting kind is twofold: <s>rasāyana</s> (rejuvenative therapy) and <s>vājīkaraṇa</s> (aphrodisiac or virilifying therapy).
The disease-destroying kind also is twofold: pacifying a disease and causing it not to arise again.
Again it is twofold: material and non-material.
There, the material kind is threefold: mineral, plant-derived, and animal-derived.
Among these, what will be stated from gold down to salts is generally mineral.
But the plant-derived kind is again fourfold, by the divisions of tree, flowering-and-fruiting tree, creeper or shrub, and herb.
There, a <s>vanaspati</s> is one that bears fruit.
A <s>vānaspatya</s> is one that has flowers and fruit.
A vine or shrub is a <s>vīrut</s>.
But an <s>auṣadhi</s> is an herb whose end comes with the ripening of its fruit.
They say that animal material is the animal-derived substance, such as honey and ghee.

The non-material kind, again, includes fasting, wind, sunshine, shade, mantra, consolation, giving, frightening, terrorizing, agitation, exhilaration, rebuke, sleep, wakefulness, massage, and the like.

children.text: punarapi ca trividhamauṣadhaṃ daivavyapāśrayaṃ yuktivyapāśrayaṃ sattvāvajayaśceti
children.translated_text: And again medicine is threefold: that based on divine means, that based on rational means, and conquest of the mind.
There, that based on divine means includes mantra, herbs, jewels, auspicious rites, offerings, oblations, observances, expiations, fasts, benedictory rites, vows, pilgrimage, and the like.
That based on rational means includes the application of diet and medicines.
Conquest of the mind, again, is restraint of the mind from what is harmful.
Again it is threefold.
It consists of removal, restoration to the natural state, and abandonment of the cause.
These, removal and the rest, are again twofold, by the division into external and internal.
There, external removal is in cases such as cysts, tumors, extra eyelashes, worms, and foreign bodies, by means of instruments, the hand, mechanical devices, and so on.
Internal removal, again, is by emesis, purgation, and the like.
Restoration to the natural state is pacification.
That, externally, includes oil massage, sudation, poultices, sprinkling, rubbing, and the like.
Internally, it is what enters inside and pacifies the doṣas without disturbing them.
Abandonment of the cause is the avoidance, according to the doṣa, of cold, heat, sitting, exercise, and the like, and the non-consumption of oily, dry, and similar things.

children.text: tatra śastrādisādhye bheṣajam anukramate na tu bheṣajasādhye śastrādi ||
children.translated_text: There, in a condition treatable by surgery and the like, medicine follows in due order; but surgery and the like do not follow in a condition treatable by medicine.

children.text: punarapi trividhaṃ hetuviparītaṃ vyādhiviparītam ubhayārthakāri ca
children.translated_text: Again it is threefold: opposite to the cause, opposite to the disease, and accomplishing both purposes.

children.text: tatra hetuviparītaṃ gurusnigdhaśītādije vyādhau laghurūkṣoṣṇādi tathetarasminnitarat
children.translated_text: There, what is opposite to the cause is light, dry, hot, and the like in a disease caused by heavy, oily, cold, and similar factors, and the corresponding opposite in the other case.

children.text: vyādhiviparītaṃ dvau mūlopakramau tau ca snehasvedau laṅghanabṛṃhaṇe
children.translated_text: What is opposite to the disease comprises the two root treatments, namely oleation and sudation, and also lightening and nourishing.
It also includes the five procedures beginning with emesis, together with fumigation, smoke inhalation, collyrium, and the like.
Likewise it includes softening, poulticing, incision, and the like.

children.text: yacca doṣaśamanatve satyapi jvare viśeṣato'bhihitaṃ mustāparpaṭakaṃ yavāgvaśca pramehe rajanī yavānnaṃ cetyādi
children.translated_text: And there are things which, though they are generally pacifiers of the doṣas, are specially prescribed in fever, such as mustā, parpaṭaka, and gruel, and in urinary disorders, such as turmeric and food made of barley, and so on.
In upward-moving <s>raktapitta</s> (bleeding disorder) there is purgation, and in downward-moving there is emesis.
What accomplishes both purposes, again, is medicine based on divine means.

children.text: tathā chardyāṃ chardanam atīsāre'nulomanaṃ madātyaye madyapānaṃ tucchadagdhe'gnipratapanaṃ pitte'ntargūḍhe vimārgage vā svedaḥ kaṭvamlalavaṇatīkṣṇoṣṇābhyavahāraśca bahiḥpravartanāya svamārgāpādanāya ca
children.translated_text: Likewise, in vomiting there is emesis; in diarrhea, downward regulation; in intoxication, drinking liquor; when one is slightly burned, heating by fire; and when pitta is hidden inside or moving on a wrong path, there is sweating and the consumption of pungent, sour, salty, sharp, and hot substances, for the sake of bringing it outward and restoring it to its own path.

children.text: śleṣmaṇi cāntarnigūḍhe stabdhe bahiḥ śītopacārastatpīḍitasyoṣmaṇo 'ntaḥpraveśena kaphavilayanāyeti
children.translated_text: And when phlegm is concealed within and congealed, external cold treatment is used so that the heat oppressed by it may enter inside and dissolve the kapha.
For such a proper medicine, being not contrary, accomplishes the purpose of being opposite to the cause and to the disease.
Non-medicine, again, is only twofold.
It is injurious and secondarily injurious.
There, what immediately takes life is injurious; what does so after a lapse of time is secondarily injurious.
After this, a portion of medicine will be taught in broad outline according to distinctions of taste, potency, and the like.
Gold is nourishing, unctuous, and sweet in taste and post-digestive effect.
It removes the defect of poison, is cooling, somewhat astringent, and is a <s>rasāyana</s>.

children.text: rūpyaṃ snigdhaṃ kaṣāyāmlaṃ vipāke madhuraṃ saram
children.translated_text: Silver is unctuous, astringent and sour, sweet in post-digestive effect, and mobile.
It preserves youth, is cooling, scraping, and conquers vāta and pitta.
Copper is somewhat bitter and sweet, astringent, scraping, and light.
It has a pungent post-digestive effect and taste, is cooling, healing, and conquers kapha and pitta.
Bronze has an astringent aftertaste, is clear, scraping, and light.
It clarifies vision, is dry, bitter, and removes pitta and kapha.
Tin, being somewhat bitter and salty, is purgative and reduces pallor, skin disease, worms, and vāta.

children.text: lekhanaṃ pittalaṃ kiṃcittrapu sīsaṃ ca tadguṇam ||
children.translated_text: It is scraping and somewhat productive of pitta; lead has those same qualities.
Black iron, too, is beneficial for the eyes, astringent, sweetish and bitter.
It is scraping, productive of vāta, cooling, and drives away worms, skin disease, and kapha.
It destroys laxity of the limbs, greying of hair, and pallor, and conquers wasting and swelling.
Sharp iron is similar, but especially so; it is diffusive and very hard to digest.
Ruby, great sapphire, topaz, and <s>vidūraka</s>,
together with pearl, coral, diamond, emerald, cat's-eye, crystal, and the like,

children.text: maṇiratnaṃ saraṃ śītaṃ kaṣāyaṃ svādu lekhanam
children.translated_text: are jewel-gems; they are mobile, cooling, astringent, sweet, and scraping.
When worn, they are beneficial for the eyes and remove sin, misfortune, and poison.
They are blessed, promote life and <s>ojas</s> (vital vigor), produce joy and enthusiasm, and are auspicious.
Glass is alkaline and hot in potency, and when used as collyrium it benefits the eyesight.
Conch and seashell are cooling, astringent, and strongly scraping.

children.text: tutthakaṃ kaṭu sakṣāraṃ kaṣāyaṃ viśadaṃ laghu ||
children.translated_text: Tutthaka is pungent, alkaline, astringent, clear, and light.
It is scraping, purgative, beneficial to the eyes, and removes itching, worms, and poison.
Gairika is clear, unctuous, astringent and sweet, and cold in potency.
Manohva removes kapha; it is bitter and pungent, scraping, and flowing.
Haritala is unctuous, astringent and pungent, and dispels poison.
Anjana is astringent, sweet, cooling, scraping, and unctuous.
It removes disorders of blood and pitta, poison, vomiting, and hiccup, and clarifies the sight.
Among these, srotoñjana is best; after it comes sauvira collyrium.
Rasanjana removes kapha, is bitter and pungent, cuts through obstructions, and is somewhat hot.
It is sweet, calms hiccup, and removes cough, urinary disorders, and wasting disease.
Shilajatu removes kapha, is hot and pungent, and is a <s>rasayana</s> (rejuvenative).

children.text: tiktaṃ ca chedanaṃ yogavāhi tat sarvarogajit
children.translated_text: It is also bitter, cutting, a carrier in combinations, and conquers all diseases.
In particular it removes dysuria, urinary disorders, piles, anemia, swelling, and kapha.
Vamsharocana is astringent, sweet, dry, and removes cough.
Tugaksiri is sweet and cooling, and removes wasting disease, dyspnea, and cough.

children.text: viṣyandi lavaṇaṃ sarvaṃ sūkṣmaṃ sṛṣṭamalaṃ mṛdu
children.translated_text: All salt is moistening, subtle, soft, and makes the feces pass freely.
It pacifies vata, ripens, is sharp and hot, stimulates taste, and increases kapha and pitta.

children.text: saindhavaṃ tatra sasvādu vṛṣyaṃ hṛdyaṃ tridoṣanut
children.translated_text: Among salts, saindhava is slightly sweet, virilizing, wholesome for the heart, and removes all three dosas.
It is light, not very hot, wholesome for the eyes, non-burning, and kindles the digestive fire.
Sauvarcala is light, wholesome for the heart, fragrant, and purifies belching.
It has a pungent post-digestive effect, removes constipation, kindles digestion, and gives appetite.
Vida salt kindles digestion and moves kapha and vata downward and upward into their proper course.
It destroys constipation, distention, obstruction, colic, and heaviness.
Sea salt is sweet in post-digestive effect, heavy, and increases phlegm.
Audbhida salt is slightly bitter and pungent, alkaline, sharp, and promotes moistening discharge.
In black salt there are the qualities of sauvarcala salt, except for fragrance.

children.text: romakaṃ laghu pāṃsūtthaṃ sakṣāraṃ śleṣmalaṃ guru ||
children.translated_text: Romaka salt is light, born from earth or dust, alkaline, phlegm-producing, and heavy.
In application, however, one should use saindhava and the other salts.
The alkali produced from barley awns pacifies abdominal tumors, heart disease, grahani disorders, anemia, spleen disease, distention, and throat diseases,
as well as dyspnea, piles, kapha, and cough.
Svarjika has those qualities in lesser degree, but exceeds it in alkalinity.
Every alkali is supremely sharp and hot, light, and destructive of worms.
It vitiates pitta and blood, ripens, cuts, is good for the heart, and splits apart.
Because of its pungency and saltiness it is unwholesome for semen, vitality, hair, and eyesight.

children.text: dīpanī pācanī medhyā vayasaḥ sthāpanī param
children.translated_text: Haritaki kindles digestion, cooks undigested matter, promotes intelligence, and is supremely stabilizing for age.
It is hot in potency, flowing, life-promoting, and gives strength to the intellect and senses.
Haritaki conquers leprosy and skin disease, discoloration, hoarseness, and chronic irregular fever,
diseases of the head and eyes, anemia, heart disease, jaundice, and grahani disorders,
wasting, swelling, diarrhea, urinary disorders, delusion, vomiting, and worms,
dyspnea, cough, salivation, piles, spleen disease, distention, poison, and abdominal enlargement,
obstruction of the channels, abdominal tumors, stiffness of the thighs, and anorexia,
and the various diseases born of kapha and vata.
Amalaka is similar to it, but cooling; because of its sweetness it is supreme in conquering pitta.
Because it has a pungent post-digestive effect it conquers kapha, and because of its sourness it conquers vata.

children.text: paraṃ ca kaṇṭhyaṃ cakṣuṣyaṃ hṛdyaṃ dāhajvarāpaham
children.translated_text: It is also excellent for the throat, beneficial to the eyes, good for the heart, and removes burning and fever.
Aksha has those qualities in lesser degree; it is astringent, sweet, and cooling.
It removes cough, dyspnea, phlegm in the throat, pitta, and semen; it is light.

children.text: paraṃ keśyastu tanmajjā śukraghnaṃ ca tato'ñjanam ||
children.translated_text: Its kernel is especially good for the hair, and the collyrium made from it is still more destructive of semen.
This triphala is the best <s>rasayana</s> (rejuvenative) and removes diseases of the eyes.
It heals, and conquers skin diseases, moisture, fat, urinary disorders, kapha, and blood disorders.

children.text: athāto rogabhedīyamadhyāyaṃ vyākhyāsyāma iti ha smāhurātreyādayo maharṣayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on the classification of diseases. Thus spoke the great seers headed by <s>Atreya</s>.
Diseases are indeed of seven kinds: innate, fetal, postnatal, traumatic, time-produced, influence-produced, and nature-produced.
Each of these, however, is separately twofold.

children.text: tatra sahajāḥ śukrārtavadoṣānvayāḥ kuṣṭhārśomehādayaḥ pitṛjā mātṛjāśca
children.translated_text: Among them, innate diseases, such as skin disease, piles, and urinary disease, follow from defects of semen and menstrual blood, and are paternal or maternal.
Fetal diseases, such as hunchbackedness, lameness, tawny coloration, and kilasa, arise from misconduct of the mother; they may be born from the food-rasa or from disturbance of pregnancy cravings.
Postnatal diseases arise from one's own misconduct, and are born of overnourishment or undernourishment.
Traumatic diseases arise from wounds, fractures, blows, anger, grief, fear, and the like, and are bodily or mental.
Time-produced diseases, such as fevers caused by cold and the like, are born of deranged seasons or of lack of protection.
Influence-produced diseases include fevers and the like caused by transgressing gods and teachers, curses, Atharvan rites, and so on, as well as beings such as pisacas.
Nature-produced diseases include hunger, thirst, old age, and the like; they are timely or untimely.
Among these, the timely ones are produced despite protection, while those born from non-protection are untimely.

children.text: ta ete samāsataḥ punardvividhā bhavanti pratyutpannakarmajāḥ pūrvakarmajāśca
children.translated_text: These again, in summary, are twofold: produced by present action and produced by former action.

children.text: tatra rogotpatti pratyutpannaṃ karma yadanenaiva śarīreṇa dṛṣṭamadṛṣṭaṃ coddiśyāptopadiṣṭānāṃ vihitānāṃ pratiṣiddhānāmananuṣṭhānamanuṣṭhānaṃ vā
children.translated_text: There, the present action that produces disease is this: with this very body, with regard to what is seen and unseen, one fails to perform what reliable authorities have taught as prescribed, or performs what they have taught as prohibited.
Former action, however, is that which belongs to a past previous birth.
That has also previously been called daiva, and is divided into fixed and unfixed.
Therefore diseases whose causes are unseen are produced by present action.
The opposite are those born from daiva.
Those with slight causes but great pain are of both kinds.
Among these, diseases of the former types are pacified by practicing the appropriate opposites in each case.
Diseases due to daiva are pacified, even while the contrary practice is present, through the exhaustion of undesirable karma.
The others are pacified through the exhaustion of the dosas and of karma.

children.text: anye tu punaḥ pratyutpannaṃ karma parakṛtamapi varṇayanti
children.translated_text: But others again describe even present action as something done by another.
And they call that an influence or conditioning produced by another.
And thus they say:

children.text: yadi svayaṃ kṛtādeva karmaṇaḥ kāryanirvṛttiḥ syāt na dṛṣṭaṃ puruṣāntarakṛtātkimiti vidvānapi parācaritayor upakārāpakārayoḥ sukhaduḥkhānurodhāt toṣaroṣau pratikartavyacintāṃ vā pratipadyate
children.translated_text: If the accomplishment of an effect came only from action done by oneself, and not, as is observed, from something done by another person, why then does even a learned man, because of pleasure and pain following on help and injury done by others, enter into satisfaction and anger, or into the thought of what ought to be done in return?
Thus these diseases, while being twofold, arise as threefold.
And from that, according to the particular doṣa, they are further sevenfold.

children.text: sakalo'pi cāyaṃ rogasamūhaḥ pratīkāravān āyurvedavihitam upadeśam apekṣate
children.translated_text: And this whole aggregate of diseases, since it has remedies, depends upon the instruction prescribed by <s>Āyurveda</s>.

children.text: yasmānniyatahetuko'pyāmayaḥ samyagbhiṣagādeśānuṣṭhānād upāttāyuḥsaṃskārāparikṣaye sati sahyavedanatāṃ pratipadyate
children.translated_text: For even an illness that has a fixed cause, when the directions of a proper physician are carried out and the acquired conditioning of lifespan has not been exhausted, becomes one whose pain can be endured.
But if it is not treated, almost every disease breaks one off prematurely.

children.text: svayamapi ca daivānnidānālpatayā vā nivartamānaḥ ṣoḍaśaguṇasamuditakriyopalambhād āśutaram aparikliṣṭasya cāpagacchati
children.translated_text: And even when it is subsiding of itself, through fate or through the slightness of its cause, it goes away more quickly and without distress to the patient when treatment endowed with the sixteen qualities is obtained.

children.text: aniyataphaladāyini tu daive hitābhyāsaratasyāvakāśameva na labhate vyādhiḥ
children.translated_text: But when destiny gives an uncertain result, disease finds no opportunity in one who is devoted to the practice of what is beneficial.

children.text: tasmānna kasyāṃcid avasthāyām ātmavān hitāhitayos tulyadarśī syāt ||
children.translated_text: Therefore in no condition should a self-controlled person regard the beneficial and the harmful as equal.
Again, diseases are threefold according to the distinction of mild, moderate, and excessive.
Among them, those with few symptoms are mild, those with middling symptoms are moderate, and those with complete symptoms are excessive.
They have again been taught earlier as fourfold according to such distinctions as being easily curable and the rest.

children.text: subahuśo 'pi ca bhidyamānā vyādhayo nijāgantutāṃ na vyabhicaranti
children.translated_text: And although diseases are divided in very many ways, they do not deviate from being endogenous or adventitious.

children.text: tatra nijāstu doṣotthāsteṣu pūrvaṃ vātādayo vaiṣamyamāpadyante tato vyathābhinirvartate
children.translated_text: There the endogenous are those arising from the doṣas; in them, first <s>vāta</s> and the others fall into imbalance, and then pain is produced.
But the adventitious are born from external causes; in them pain first arises, and after that imbalance of the doṣas.

children.text: doṣavaiṣamyeṇaiva ca bahurūpā ruganubadhyate pravardhate ca
children.translated_text: And through imbalance of the doṣas, pain of many forms is connected with the disease and increases.

children.text: evaṃ ca kṛtvā na doṣavyatirekeṇa rogānubandhaḥ kevalaṃ paurvāparye viśeṣaḥ
children.translated_text: Thus, accordingly, there is no continuation of disease apart from the doṣas; the distinction is only one of earlier and later occurrence.

children.text: tasmādekākārā eva rogāstathā ruksāmānyādasaṃkhyabhedā vā pratyekaṃ samutthānasthānasaṃsthānadharmanāmavedanā prabhāvopakramaviśeṣātte yathāsthūlaṃ yathāsvamevopadekṣyante
children.translated_text: Therefore diseases are of one form, because pain is common to them; or they have innumerable divisions, each according to differences of origin, location, configuration, properties, name, sensation, specific effect, and treatment. They will be taught, in a broad way, each according to its own nature.
And because they are innumerable, one should classify diseases and their treatment precisely by the signs of the doṣas.
For the doṣas alone are the single cause of all diseases.

children.text: yathaiva śakuniḥ sarvataḥ paripatan divasaṃ svāṃ chāyāṃ nātivartate
children.translated_text: Just as a bird, flying about everywhere during the day, does not pass beyond its own shadow,

children.text: yathā vā kṛtsnaṃ vikārajātaṃ vaiśvarūpyeṇa vyavasthitaṃ guṇatrayamavyatiricya vartate tathaivedamapi kṛtsnaṃ vikārajātaṃ doṣatrayamiti
children.translated_text: or just as the whole class of transformations, established in manifold form, exists without going beyond the three <s>guṇas</s>, so too this whole class of transformations is nothing but the three doṣas.

children.text: yathā ca vidyudvarṣādayo nabhasi bhavanti na tvavaśyaṃ nimittatastvavaśyamapi
children.translated_text: And just as lightning, rain, and the like occur in the sky, not necessarily from a visible occasion, though from some occasion they necessarily do occur,
and waves, bubbles, and the like occur in water, so diseases occur in the doṣas.

children.text: trividhaṃ tu nimittameṣām asātmyendriyārthasaṃyogaḥ prajñāparādhaḥ pariṇāmaśca
children.translated_text: Their cause, however, is threefold: unsuitable conjunction of sense faculties with their objects, failure of judgment, and transformation.

children.text: te punaḥ pratyekam atiyogāyogamithyāyogabhedāt tridhā bhidyante
children.translated_text: These again are each divided threefold by the distinctions of excessive use, non-use, and wrong use.

children.text: tatra yathāsvaṃ cakṣurādīndriyāṇāṃ rūpādibhirarthairatisaṃsargo'tiyogaḥ alpaśo naiva vā saṃsargastvayogaḥ
children.translated_text: There, with respect to each, excessive contact of the eye and the other sense faculties with forms and the other objects is excessive use; slight contact, or none at all, is non-use.
Seeing things that are minute, too distant, too near, too bright, terrifying, disagreeable, distorted, and the like,
hearing what is hateful, too loud, harsh, frightening, and the like,
smelling what is putrid, impure, excessively sharp, fierce, adverse, and the like,

children.text: svabhāvādibhir āhārakalpanāviśeṣāyatanair apathyānāṃ rasānāmabhyavahārastathā snānādīnāṃ śītoṣṇādīnāṃ ca spṛśyānām ayathāvadupasevanam aśucibhūtābhighrātaviṣavātādisaṃsparśaśca mithyāyogaḥ ||
children.translated_text: eating unsuitable tastes through special arrangements and bases of food preparation, according to their nature and so on; likewise improper use of tangible things such as bathing and cold or heat; and contact with filth, beings, wounds, poison, wind, and the like: this is wrong use.
But unwholesome action, threefold by the division of body, speech, and mind, is failure of judgment.
There, excessive activity of bodily action and the like is excessive use.
Little activity, or none at all, is non-use.

children.text: vegodīraṇadhāraṇaviṣamāṅgaceṣṭanaskhalanakaṇḍūyanaprahāraprāṇāyāmādi tathā kṣutpipāsārdhabhuktabhāṣaṇādi bhayaśokerṣyāmātsaryādi daśadhiyaṃ cākuśalaṃ karma yathāsvaṃ mithyāyogaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Forcing or suppressing natural urges, uneven movements of the limbs, stumbling, scratching, striking, breath-control and the like; likewise speaking when hungry, thirsty, or half-fed and so on; fear, grief, jealousy, envy, and the ten unskillful actions of the intellect, each in its own sphere, are wrong use.

children.text: pariṇāmaḥ punaḥ kāla ucyate so'pi śītoṣṇavarṣabhedāttridhā
children.translated_text: Transformation, again, is called time; it too is threefold by the division of cold, heat, and rain.
There, a season having its own marks in excessive measure is excessive use.
One whose own marks are deficient is non-use.
One that is contrary is wrong use.
These, namely excessive use and the rest, are in general characterized by being non-alleviating.

children.text: sarvo vā prajñāparādha evāyaṃ yadeṣām avivarjanam
children.translated_text: Or rather all this is simply failure of judgment, namely the failure to avoid them.
Objects, actions, and times, on the other hand, when properly joined, are for the most part causes of health because they are alleviating.

children.text: tatrāpi rasavarjā viṣayā yathāyathamindriyaṃ bādhante'nugṛhṇanti ca
children.translated_text: Among them, the objects, except for tastes, harm and benefit the corresponding sense faculty as appropriate.
But the remaining ones, tastes, actions, and times, affect the whole body.
Moreover:
One should not determine the presence or absence of all states apart from proper conjunction, excessive conjunction, and the like.
And for all disorders, specific forms of presence and absence arise from the specific character of cause, doṣa, and affected tissue.

children.text: yadā hyete trayo nidānādiviśeṣānnānyo 'nyam anubadhnantīṣad vānubadhnantyabalā vā na tadābhinirvartante vyādhayaścirād vābhinirvartante tanavo vā bhavantyasaṃpūrṇaliṅgā vā viparīte tu viparītāḥ ||
children.translated_text: For when these three, because of distinctions beginning with causes, do not bind themselves to one another, or bind themselves only slightly, or are weak, then diseases do not arise; or they arise after a long time, or are slight, or have incomplete symptoms. But when the opposite is the case, the opposite results occur.

children.text: trayaśca rogāṇāṃ mārgā bāhyamadhyābhyantarāstatra bāhyo raktādidhātavastvakca
children.translated_text: And there are three pathways of diseases: external, middle, and internal. There, the external consists of the blood and other tissues and the skin.
This, again, is called the branch pathway.

Based in it are goiter, pustules, alaji, apacī, skin-tags, tumors, overgrowth of flesh, moles, vyaṅga, and the like, and also external swellings, piles, abdominal tumors, erysipelas, abscesses, and the like.
The middle pathway consists of vital spots such as the head, heart, and bladder, and of bones and joints.
Attached there are the ligaments, vessels, tendons, and the like.

Based in it are hemiplegia, seizures, convulsive apatanaka and related disorders, consumption, diseases of bones and joints, prolapse of the rectum, and the like, as well as diseases of the head and so on.

children.text: ābhyantaro mahāsrotaḥ śarīramadhyaṃ mahānimnamāmapakvāśayāśrayaḥ koṣṭho'ntariti paryāyāḥ
children.translated_text: The internal pathway is the great channel, the middle of the body, the great hollow, the seat of the stomach and intestines; koṣṭha and antara are synonyms.

Based in it are fever, diarrhea, vomiting, alasaka, cholera-like visūcikā, dyspnea, cough, hiccup, ānāha, abdominal enlargement, spleen disease, and the like, and also internal swellings, piles, abscesses, abdominal tumors, and the like.

children.text: te ca rogāḥ svapradhānā bhavantyanyaparivārā vā kramād ananubandhānubandhākhyāḥ
children.translated_text: And those diseases may be principal in themselves or surrounded by others; respectively they are called unconnected and connected.
Among them, the first are independent, have clear forms, and each has its own cause and alleviating factor.
The others, however, are the opposite of these.
The doṣas too are the same in that respect.
Among these, diseases surrounded by others are of two kinds: those that go before and those that follow after.
Of them, the first are designated prodromal signs, while the others are complications.
One should recognize them precisely as they will be described in each case.
When the principal disease is pacified, they are pacified.
Or, if they are not pacified, one should treat them afterward.
Or one should quickly treat a strong complication, provided this does not conflict with the principal treatment.

children.text: sa hi pīḍākarataro bhavati vyādhiparikliṣṭadehatvāt pramehapiḍikādivat
children.translated_text: For it becomes more painful, because the body has already been afflicted by disease, as with diabetic eruptions and the like.

children.text: tathānyaḥ pradhāna eva rogo'nyasya heturbhavati yathā jvaro raktapittasya raktapittaṃ vā jvarasya
children.translated_text: Likewise, another principal disease itself becomes the cause of another, as fever may be the cause of hemorrhagic pitta, or hemorrhagic pitta of fever.
Those two may be the cause of dyspnea; spleen disease may be the cause of abdominal enlargement.
That may be the cause of swelling.
Piles may be the cause of abdominal tumor, abdominal enlargement, diarrhea, and grahaṇī disorder.
Catarrh may be the cause of cough and fever.
Those two may be the cause of wasting; wasting may be the cause of emaciating consumption.

children.text: ekaścāpacāro nimittamekasya vyādheḥ bahūnāṃ ca tathā bahavaḥ
children.translated_text: One offense may be the occasion for one disease and also for many; likewise many offenses may be the occasion.
In the same way there may be one symptom.
So too the very same measure may be a means of pacification in one case and, likewise, a cause of aggravation in another.
Therefore, being attentive, one should examine them properly by authoritative teaching and the other means.

children.text: tatrāgamato rogamevamevaṃ prakopanamevaṃ yonimevamātmānam evam adhiṣṭhānamevaṃ vedanamevaṃ rūpaśabdagandharasasparśam evaṃ pūrvarūpamevamupadravamevaṃ vṛddhisthānakṣayānvitamevam udarkam evaṃnāmānam
children.translated_text: There, from authoritative teaching one knows that a disease is of such and such a kind, has such and such aggravation, such and such source, such and such nature, such and such site, such and such sensation, such and such color, sound, smell, taste, and touch, such and such prodrome, such and such complication, such and such increase, stability, and decrease, such and such outcome, and such and such name.
In that case, this is the undertaking of counteraction, and otherwise there is abstention from it.

By direct perception, however, one should examine the patient with the appropriate senses: color, shape, measure, build, complexion, excess of feces, urine, and vomit, intestinal gurgling, cracking of the finger-joints and the like, the smell of the body, feces, wounds, and so on, and the touch as numb, cold, hot, stiff, throbbing, smooth, or rough.

children.text: prakṛtivikṛtibhuktam āsyarasaṃ tu praśnena tathā suchardaduśchardatvaṃ mṛdukrūrakoṣṭhatāṃ svapnadarśanamabhiprāyaṃ janmāmayapravṛttinakṣatradviṣṭeṣṭasukhaduḥkhāni ca
children.translated_text: But the natural and altered taste in the mouth after eating should be known by questioning, and so too ease or difficulty in vomiting, softness or hardness of the bowel, dreams seen, intentions, birth, onset of illness, asterism, dislikes and likes, pleasures and pains.
Likewise age is known by direct perception as well.

children.text: anumānatastu yūkāpasarpaṇena śarīrasya vairasyaṃ makṣikopasarpaṇena mādhuryaṃ tathāgniṃ jaraṇaśaktyā balaṃ vyāyāmaśaktyā gūḍhaliṅgaṃ vyādhimupaśayānupaśayato doṣapramāṇam upacāraviśeṣeṇāyuṣaḥ kṣayaṃ riṣṭaiḥ
children.translated_text: By inference, one knows unpleasantness of the body from lice moving away, sweetness from flies approaching, digestive fire from the power of digestion, strength from the capacity for exercise, a disease whose signs are hidden from what relieves or does not relieve it, the amount of doṣa from the special kind of treatment, and the loss of life-span from ominous signs.
And one knows constitution, mental firmness, excellence of tissues, suitability, and strength by habitual practice and observation.
He who does not enter, like a yogin, with the lamp of knowledge and intelligence,
into the inner self of the patient, does not treat diseases.
These two diseased persons do not reveal the true nature of the disease:
one is a serious disease which, because it rests on strength of mind and body,
appears like a light disease; and the light disease appears otherwise than that.
A fool is deluded about the two merely by the external member.
Then, applying a small, weak, contrary, or otherwise unsuitable
regimen when the opposite is required, he steals away the lives of patients.

children.text: jñānāṃśena na hi jñānaṃ kṛtsne jñeye pravartate
children.translated_text: For knowledge that is only a portion of knowledge does not operate upon the whole knowable object.
Therefore the physician should desire to know the truth through study of the treatise.
But one who is constantly diligent, having considered everything in every way,

children.text: na jātu skhalati prājño viṣame'pi kriyāpathe ||
children.translated_text: being wise, never stumbles even on a difficult path of treatment.
An adventitious disorder follows an innate disorder, and likewise an innate disorder follows an adventitious one when it has become greatly increased.

children.text: tatrānubandhaṃ prakṛtiṃ ca samyak jñātvā tataḥ karma samārabheta ||
children.translated_text: There, having properly understood the connection and the original condition, one should then begin the treatment.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on the administration of medicines.
Thus spoke the great seers headed by <s>Atreya</s>.
When administering medicine, one should first of all examine the patient beforehand.

children.text: kasminnayaṃ deśe jātaḥ saṃvṛddho vyādhito vā
children.translated_text: In what region was this person born, brought up, or afflicted by disease?

children.text: tasmiṃśca deśe manuṣyāṇāmidamāhārajātamidaṃ vihārajātametāvadbalam evaṃvidhaṃ sattvamevaṃvidhaṃ sātmyamiyaṃ bhaktirime vyādhayo hitamidamahitamidamiti
children.translated_text: And in that region, among the people, one should know: this is the kind of diet, this is the kind of regimen, this much is their strength, such is their mental constitution, such is what they are accustomed to, this is their preference, these are their diseases, this is wholesome, and this is unwholesome.

children.text: prāyograhaṇena kena vā nidānaviśeṣeṇāsya kupito doṣo doṣasya hyekasyāpi bahavaḥ prakope hetavaḥ
children.translated_text: By the word “generally,” one should also determine by what particular cause this person's <s>doṣa</s> has been aggravated; for even a single <s>doṣa</s> has many causes of aggravation.
Therefore one should understand the <s>doṣa</s> in this way, by means of its own characteristic signs, by its actions, and also by reasoned judgment.

children.text: tadyathā kimāhāreṇa kupito vāyuḥ kiṃ vihāreṇa tathā rūkṣeṇa laghunā śiśireṇa vā sāhasena vegarodhena vā bhayena śokena veti
children.translated_text: For example: was <s>vāyu</s> aggravated by diet, or by regimen; likewise by something dry, light, or cold; or by overexertion, suppression of natural urges, fear, or grief?
